parts: Supply of a commodity is the quantity that a seller offers for sale at a given price in a given period of time. Like demand, the definition has three parts: quantity, price and time. Example: Ganga Singh sold 120 litres of milk at ₹25 a litre last week.
Firms — farmers, manufacturers and sellers — supply goods. A good being available in the market does not mean it has been supplied.

Stock is the total quantity a seller has at a particular point of time. Supply is the part of the stock the seller is ready to sell at a given price during a period of time. Stock is measured at a point of time; supply is a flow, measured over a period. Example: a grain merchant has a stock of 820 quintals of rice on 1 August and supplies 300 quintals at ₹2,300 during August.
(1) Price of the commodity: a higher price means higher AR and TR, so more is supplied.
(2) Technology: better technology lowers the cost per unit and raises profit, so supply increases. Old technology raises cost and lowers supply.
(3) Price of inputs: if milk becomes cheaper, ice cream costs less to make and its supply rises. Dearer inputs reduce supply.
(4) Prices of other related goods: if the price of rice rises, a farmer shifts land from wheat to rice, so rice supply rises and wheat supply falls.
(5) Objective of the firm: a firm that wants to maximise sales may supply more even at a lower price. Other firms aim at profit, goodwill or employment.
(6) Government policy: a higher tax (VAT, excise or sales tax) raises cost and reduces supply. A tax cut or subsidy increases supply.
Supply schedule and law of supply
An individual supply schedule is a table of the quantities one firm supplies at different prices. X Ltd's sugar: ₹2,800 – 8 quintals; ₹2,900 – 9; ₹3,000 – 10; ₹3,100 – 12; ₹3,200 – 15.
Law of supply: other factors remaining constant, the price of a commodity and its quantity supplied are directly (positively) related. More is supplied at a higher price and less at a lower price.

The supply curve is the diagram of the law of supply, with price on the Y-axis and quantity on the X-axis. It slopes upward from left to right, for three reasons. (1) A higher price brings higher profit, so firms supply more. (2) A higher price makes sellers release part of their stock. (3) Higher profit attracts new firms into the market.

Market supply is the total quantity all firms offer at a given price and time — the sum of individual supplies. At ₹2,800, firms X, Y and Z supply 8, 10 and 15 quintals, so market supply = 33 quintals.

Market supply depends on the factors behind individual supply, plus two more. (1) Number of firms: more firms means more supply. (2) Expected future price: if prices are expected to rise, firms supply less now; if they are expected to fall, firms supply more now.
